terms.gloss: it is worth while, worth the trouble
evidence: Ter. And. 217: audīreque eōrum est operae pretium audāciam
Plaut. Mil. 31b: nē hercle operae pretium quidemst
Traupman 409: it is worthwhile, operae pretium est; it isn’t worth it, nōn est operae pretium
Traupman 105: it pays to listen, pretium operae est auscultāre
terms.comment: “The pay for the work”; operae pretium facere, to do something worth the effort (Liv. praef. 1).

terms.gloss: it is worth it (the price, the trouble)
terms.grammar: phrase: genitive of value; nōn est tantī, it isn’t worth it
evidence: Cic. Cat. 1.22: sed est tantī, dum modo tua ista sit prīvāta calamitās
Gell. 1.8.6: ego paenitēre tantī nōn emō
Traupman 409: it’s not worth all that, tantī nōn est

terms.grammar: adjective, with the ablative, a supine in -ū, or quī and the subjunctive
evidence: Liv. 4.30.4: nihil dignum dictū āctum hīs cōnsulibus
Ter. Eun. 311: sīve adeō digna rēs est ubi tū nervōs intendās tuōs
terms.comment: With an infinitive only in verse and post-Augustan prose (Lewis & Short): Horātius ferē sōlus legī dignus, almost the only one worth reading (Quint. 10.1.96).

terms.gloss: be worth nothing, be a good-for-nothing (of a person)
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 3.77: accēpimus eum nihil hominis esse, a worthless fellow (Lewis & Short s.v. nihil)
Traupman 112: nihil est, he’s worth nothing
terms.comment: Of a person, “he is nothing”: Latin uses the plain verb where English speaks of worth.

phrases.latin: Nē hercle operae pretium quidemst mihi tē narrāre tuās quī virtūtēs sciam.
phrases.english: Really, it isn’t even worth your telling me of your exploits: I know them already.
I don’t pay that much for something I’ll regret

phrases.latin: nihil dignum dictū āctum hīs cōnsulibus
phrases.english: nothing worth telling happened in their year
